A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Robot-R1 and retain matching methods, experiments and supporting material. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Robot-R1 and SFT experiments on Robot-R1 Bench, EmbodiedBench Manipulation and SpatialRGPT-Bench, together with ablations and qualitative results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds human assessment, optimizer and seed comparisons, transfer evaluations, and simulated and physical robot-control experiments.

M1.justification: The core MCQA construction, auxiliary tasks, rewards and GRPO procedure remain unchanged. v2 adds limited adaptations: supervised initialization before Robot-R1 in Appendix C and a diffusion-policy head attached to the LVLM for downstream control in Appendix F. Renaming primitive movement and subtask reasoning does not change their underlying procedures.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained benchmarks, v2 evaluates real demonstration images from BridgeV2, VLABench reasoning categories, LIBERO manipulation tasks and four physical pick-and-place tasks using a Franka Research 3 arm. These substantially extend the represented environments and task requirements, including actual physical execution.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated RLOO and REINFORCE++ alternatives to GRPO in Table 7 and a high-quality CoT-SFT comparator in Table 13. The latter uses GPT-4.1-mini-generated reasoning rather than the original scripted supervision. These extend comparison to alternative RL optimizers and a different supervised-training regime; the original comparator sets remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 revises the reported training budget from one to five epochs; the training-curve caption changes Open-End/MCQA budgets from two/one to ten/five epochs. This establishes changed reporting, not that retained experiments were rerun. New protocols include blind scoring of 80 responses by eight experts, one-epoch Appendix C experiments, 50 rollouts per LIBERO task and 24 trials per physical task. Appendix C's one-epoch statement conflicts with Figure 11's blanket five-epoch description.

E4.justification: v2 adds studies of automatic-judge agreement with experts, dependence on the RL optimizer, sensitivity to sampling seeds, and RL following high-quality SFT initialization. These address evaluation validity and training robustness beyond v1's retained auxiliary-task and question-format ablations. The original qualitative examples are retained.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly reports two additional sampling-seed runs and presents individual results, means and standard deviations across three seeds in Table 8. Table 6 also introduces Pearson correlations against median ratings from eight experts. v1 contains neither practice; v2 does not provide confidence intervals or a formal significance test supporting its significance language.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and QA-ablation values remain unchanged, while Tables 6–8 and 11–15 add substantial results. These include planning judge correlation of 0.3315 versus approximately 0.89 for other categories, mixed VLABench transfer, and new baseline-versus-Robot-R1 control averages of 69.0% versus 71.8% on LIBERO and 16.67% versus 23.96% on the physical robot. These are newly reported comparisons, not performance gains between versions.

T1.justification: The state and waypoint definitions, GRPO objective, reward construction and open-ended reward formula retain their mathematical substance. Notation cleanup introduces no new assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the claims of RL-enhanced embodied reasoning, the Robot-R1 benchmark, advantages over SFT and strong low-level reasoning relative to commercial models. The added evaluations supply evidence for these claims without materially redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for weak planning-judge agreement, optimizer differences, limited low-level transfer to Bridge images, VLABench failures and the LIBERO object-category decline. These materially expand applicability boundaries and mechanism hypotheses. It also introduces strong seed-robustness interpretations, although Table 8 does not show improvement for every task and seed. The original xyz-only limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 documents the high-quality SFT data-generation procedure and adds the GR00T-N1.5 implementation reference, diffusion-head training budgets, batch size, robot platform, demonstration counts and rollout counts. Appendix B.1 changes the stated 12-hour training account from one to five epochs while retaining the same hardware. These substantially expand implementation information without establishing a new code release.

R1.justification: References 64–70 add work supporting RLOO, REINFORCE++, BridgeData V2, VLABench, GPT-4.1, GR00T-N1.5 and LIBERO. These contextualize the new experiments, while the original related-work discussion and principal novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 standardizes terminology, corrects some wording and updates affiliations, the conference header and acknowledgements. It introduces additional appendix sections and moves the original qualitative material from Appendix C to E. The existing main narrative is largely retained rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands quantitative presentation with tables for judge agreement, optimizers, seeds, transfer, cold start and VLA control. Existing tables are renumbered and restyled. v1 Figure 4 is removed, but its MCQA curves remain in the combined appendix plot, matched from v1 Figure 12 to v2 Figure 11.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses two important gaps in v1: unvalidated automatic grading and the absence of physical robot-control evaluation. Human agreement measurements, optimizer and seed studies, and downstream control experiments strengthen the empirical basis, while mixed transfer outcomes expose limitations. Inconsistent epoch reporting and overstated robustness language remain weaknesses, but the added validation and practical testing provide a clear net improvement.
